claims.evidence: This is supported by whole genome bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: The majority of CHG DMRs (>99%, in each lineage) were hypermethylated CHG DMRs in AtCMT3 expressing lineages relative to wild type.
claims.source: The majority of CHG DMRs (>99%, in each lineage) were hypermethylated CHG DMRs in AtCMT3 expressing lineages relative to wild type (Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by DMR analysis of bisulfite sequencing data.

claims.claim: Many of the CG and CHH DMRs were hypermethylated DMRs in AtCMT3 expressing lines relative to wild type and overlapped with CHG DMRs.
claims.source: Many of the CG and CHH DMRs (between 45–72% CG and 86–98% CHH, depending on the line) were also hypermethylated DMRs in AtCMT3 expressing lines relative to wild type, and overlapped with CHG DMRs, suggesting they result from cross-talk between CMT3-mediated CHG methylation and other pathways (Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by DMR analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: CG and CHH hypermethylation in AtCMT3 lines results from cross-talk between CMT3-mediated CHG methylation and other pathways.
claims.source: Many of the CG and CHH DMRs (between 45–72% CG and 86–98% CHH, depending on the line) were also hypermethylated DMRs in AtCMT3 expressing lines relative to wild type, and overlapped with CHG DMRs, suggesting they result from cross-talk between CMT3-mediated CHG methylation and other pathways (Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the overlap of DMRs in different contexts.

claims.claim: There was a significant overlap of hypermethylated CHG DMRs between all individuals.
claims.source: There was also a significant overlap of hypermethylated CHG DMRs between all individuals, suggesting that AtCMT3 was not methylating DNA randomly (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: AtCMT3 was not methylating DNA randomly.
claims.source: There was also a significant overlap of hypermethylated CHG DMRs between all individuals, suggesting that AtCMT3 was not methylating DNA randomly (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the significant overlap of DMRs between individuals.

claims.claim: There is a significant correlation between the levels of AtCMT3 expression and genome-wide CHG methylation levels (R2 = 0.8828, p=1.669×10−4).
claims.source: The results demonstrated a significant correlation between the levels of AtCMT3 expression and genome-wide CHG methylation levels (R2 = 0.8828, p=1.669×10−4, Figure 1—figure supplement 5, see Supplementary file 4 for FPKM values).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: Expression of the AtCMT3 transgene was progressively lost in the AtCMT3-L2 lineage following the T4 generation.
claims.source: These results also revealed that expression of the AtCMT3 transgene was progressively lost in the AtCMT3-L2 lineage following the T4 generation (Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing declining AtCMT3 expression.

claims.claim: The majority of CHG DMRs (18,812/25,096 or 75%) were characterized by the presence of low levels of CHG methylation in wild type that increased upon the expression of AtCMT3.
claims.source: Results showed that the majority of CHG DMRs (18,812/25,096 or 75%) were characterized by the presence of low levels of CHG methylation in wild type that increased upon the expression of AtCMT3 (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by DMR analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: 19,576 out of 25,096 (78%) total CHG DMRs overlapped with repetitive elements or intergenic regions.
claims.source: Characterizing the DMRs based on overlap with genomic features revealed that 19,576 out of 25,096 (78%) total CHG DMRs overlapped with repetitive elements or intergenic regions, which are expected targets of all DNA methylation pathways (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by genomic feature annotation of DMRs shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Plants expressing AtCMT3 exhibited increased CHG methylation over repetitive elements from ~15% methylation in wild type to ~30–70% methylation in AtCMT3 lines.
claims.source: Summarizing CHG methylation over all repetitive elements confirmed that plants expressing AtCMT3 exhibited increased CHG methylation over these regions from ~15% methylation in wild type to ~30–70% methylation in AtCMT3 lines (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by metaplot analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: A subset of regions (6,284 out of 25,096 (25%) CHG DMRs) that gained CHG methylation in AtCMT3-expressing lines had no pre-existing CHG methylation.
claims.source: In addition to methylated regions, a subset of regions (6,284 out of 25,096 (25%) CHG DMRs) that gained CHG methylation in AtCMT3-expressing lines had no pre-existing CHG methylation, and the majority (4,725/6,284 or 75%) of these regions overlapped annotated genes (Figure 1B, Figure 2A, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by DMR analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The majority (4,725/6,284 or 75%) of CHG DMRs with no pre-existing CHG methylation overlapped annotated genes.
claims.source: In addition to methylated regions, a subset of regions (6,284 out of 25,096 (25%) CHG DMRs) that gained CHG methylation in AtCMT3-expressing lines had no pre-existing CHG methylation, and the majority (4,725/6,284 or 75%) of these regions overlapped annotated genes (Figure 1B, Figure 2A, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by genomic feature annotation of DMRs.

claims.claim: Plants expressing AtCMT3 showed increases in CHG methylation over gene bodies, ranging from ~2–10% CHG methylation on average.
claims.source: Examination of percent CHG methylation over all annotated genes revealed increases in CHG methylation over gene bodies, ranging from ~2–10% CHG methylation on average, compared to no CHG methylation in wild-type plants (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by metaplot analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The patterns of CHG methylation in several generations of the AtCMT3-L2 lineage were reminiscent of that seen for gbM, with highest percent methylation levels towards the center of the gene bodies.
claims.source: The patterns of CHG methylation in several of the generations of the AtCMT3-L2 lineage, which exhibited higher levels of AtCMT3 transgene expression (Supplementary file 4), were reminiscent of that seen for gbM (Bewick and Schmitz, 2017), in that the percent methylation levels were highest towards the center of the gene bodies, decreasing towards the transcription start sites (TSS) and transcription termination sites (TTS) (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by metaplot analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: In AtCMT3-L1, the number of CHG-gain genes generally increased over generational time from 99 genes in T1 to 583 genes in T6.
claims.source: In AtCMT3-L1, the number of CHG-gain genes generally increased over generational time from 99 genes in T1 to 583 genes in T6 (Figure 2D, Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: This is supported by CHG-gain gene analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: AtCMT3-L2 individuals were characterized by higher numbers of CHG-gain genes relative to AtCMT3-L1.
claims.source: AtCMT3-L2 individuals were characterized by higher numbers of CHG-gain genes relative to AtCMT3-L1, with the T1 generation showing gains in 718 genes, 2,996 genes in T2, 3,553 genes in T3, and 4,055 genes in T4 (Figure 2D, Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: This is supported by CHG-gain gene analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Following the T4 generation, the T5 and T6 generations of AtCMT3-L2 showed a decline in the number of CHG-gain genes, with 1,937 in T5 and only 88 genes in T6.
claims.source: Following the T4 generation, the T5 and T6 generations of AtCMT3-L2 showed a decline in the number of CHG-gain genes, with 1,937 in T5 and only 88 genes in T6 (Figure 2D, Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: This is supported by CHG-gain gene analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: The overlap of CHG-gain genes between all individuals was significantly higher than expected by chance.
claims.source: Despite the variation in the number of CHG-gain genes, the overlap of CHG-gain genes between all individuals was significantly higher than expected by chance (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The levels of AtCMT3 expression and number of CHG-gain genes were correlated (R2 = 0.7951, p=0.001).
claims.source: Indeed, based on RNA-seq assessment of AtCMT3 expression, the levels of AtCMT3 expression and number CHG-gain genes were correlated (R2 = 0.7951, p=0.001) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Two T2 generation individuals of the AtCMT3-L3 lineage had the highest AtCMT3 expression and the highest number of CHG-gain genes.
claims.source: Again, two T2 generation individuals of the AtCMT3-L3 lineage, which had the highest AtCMT3 expression (Supplementary file 4), also had the highest number of CHG-gain genes (5,566 and 6,346 CHG-gain genes for AtCMT3-L3T2 and T2b, respectively) (Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and CHG-gain gene analysis.

claims.claim: The decline in the number of CHG-gain genes in the AtCMT3-L2T5 and T6 generations is correlated with the progressive loss of AtCMT3 transgene expression.
claims.source: Therefore, the decline in the number of CHG-gain genes in the AtCMT3-L2T5 and T6 generations is correlated with the progressive loss of AtCMT3 transgene expression.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between AtCMT3 expression and CHG-gain genes.

claims.claim: Regions enriched for H3K9me2 in wild type showed increased CHG methylation in all lines expressing AtCMT3.
claims.source: Consistent with CMT3 binding of H3K9me2, regions enriched for H3K9me2 in wild type showed increased CHG methylation in all lines expressing AtCMT3 (Figure 3A–B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq and bisulfite sequencing data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claims.claim: Plants expressing AtCMT3 showed enrichment for H3K9me2 across H3K9me2 ChIP peaks identified in wild type, but there were no further increases of H3K9me2 in heterochromatin.
claims.source: We found plants expressing AtCMT3 also showed enrichment for H3K9me2 across H3K9me2 ChIP peaks identified in wild type, but there were no further increases of H3K9me2 in heterochromatin, despite the increase in CHG methylation (Figure 3A,C–F, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3C-F.

claims.claim: Gains in CHG methylation over gene bodies in AtCMT3-expressing lines were not associated with pre-existing H3K9me2 in wild-type plants.
claims.source: In contrast to repeat regions, gains in CHG methylation over gene bodies in AtCMT3-expressing lines were not associated with pre-existing H3K9me2 in wild-type plants (Figure 3A,C–F, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3C-F.

claims.claim: The establishment of CHG methylation following AtCMT3 expression did not result in detectable H3K9me2 across CHG-gain genes.
claims.source: Also unexpected, the establishment of CHG methylation following AtCMT3 expression did not result in detectable H3K9me2 across CHG-gain genes (Figure 3A,C–F, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3C-F.

claims.claim: H3K9me1 was enriched over regions characterized by H3K9me2.
claims.source: Similar to findings in A. thaliana (Jackson et al., 2004), H3K9me1 was enriched over regions characterized by H3K9me2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-B.

claims.claim: H3K9me1 was preferentially enriched in heterochromatin relative to CHG-gain genes before or after introduction of the transgene.
claims.source: H3K9me1 was preferentially enriched in heterochromatin relative to CHG-gain genes before or after introduction of the transgene and the H3K9me1 signal over CHG-gain genes was indistinguishable from genes that remained unmethylated (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B-C.

claims.claim: The H3K9me1 signal over CHG-gain genes was indistinguishable from genes that remained unmethylated.
claims.source: H3K9me1 was preferentially enriched in heterochromatin relative to CHG-gain genes before or after introduction of the transgene and the H3K9me1 signal over CHG-gain genes was indistinguishable from genes that remained unmethylated (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B-C.

claims.claim: Gains of CHG methylation at genic loci resulting from expression of AtCMT3 are not associated with stable H3K9 methylation.
claims.source: Overall, we conclude that gains of CHG methylation at genic loci resulting from expression of AtCMT3 are not associated with stable H3K9 methylation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on ChIP-seq data showing no H3K9me enrichment over CHG-gain genes.

claims.claim: In each line there was only a small proportion of CHG-gain genes (less than or equal to 10%) that showed a greater than two log2 fold change in expression.
claims.source: In each line there was only a small proportion of CHG-gain genes (less than or equal to 10%) that showed a greater than two log2 fold change and a similar number were both down and up-regulated (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: A similar number of CHG-gain genes were both down and up-regulated.
claims.source: In each line there was only a small proportion of CHG-gain genes (less than or equal to 10%) that showed a greater than two log2 fold change and a similar number were both down and up-regulated (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: There was no relationship between the levels of CHG methylation gain and expression changes.
claims.source: There was also no relationship between the levels of CHG methylation gain and expression changes (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: CHG gain genes were not significantly enriched in either up- or down-regulated genes (p>0.05, Fishers exact test).
claims.source: Additionally, we defined up- and down-regulated genes genome wide in AtCMT3-expressing lines (defined as greater than a two log2 fold change relative to wild type), and CHG gain genes were not significantly enriched in either up- or down-regulated genes (p>0.05, Fishers exact test) (Supplementary file 6 and Supplementary file 7).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Many of the enriched GO terms for up- and down-regulated genes were involved in abiotic stress responses.
claims.source: We found that many of the enriched terms for up- and down-regulated genes were involved in abiotic stress responses (Supplementary file 8).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis.

claims.claim: There were no consistently identified GO-term enrichments across lineages.
claims.source: However, there were no consistently identified GO-term enrichments across lineages suggesting that AtCMT3 expression was unlikely the direct or indirect cause of these changes (Supplementary file 8).
claims.evidence: This is supported by GO enrichment analysis across multiple lineages.

claims.claim: AtCMT3 expression was unlikely the direct or indirect cause of expression changes.
claims.source: However, there were no consistently identified GO-term enrichments across lineages suggesting that AtCMT3 expression was unlikely the direct or indirect cause of these changes (Supplementary file 8).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of consistent GO term enrichments.

claims.claim: Lack of transcriptional changes directly related to CHG methylation is consistent with the lack of stable H3K9me2 at these loci.
claims.source: Lack of transcriptional changes directly related to CHG methylation is consistent with the lack of stable H3K9me2 at these loci (Figure 3C–F).
claims.evidence: This is an inference connecting the expression and ChIP-seq data.

claims.claim: Genic CHG methylation in AtCMT3-expressing lines is uncoupled from heterochromatin formation and transcriptional silencing, similar to gbM.
claims.source: We conclude that genic CHG methylation in AtCMT3-expressing lines is uncoupled from heterochromatin formation and transcriptional silencing, similar to gbM.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the lack of H3K9me2 and expression changes.

claims.claim: Among the generations of AtCMT3-L1 and L2, there was a total of 4,769 CHG-gain genes identified in at least one individual.
claims.source: Among the generations of AtCMT3-L1 and L2, there was a total of 4,769 CHG-gain genes identified in at least one individual (Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: This is supported by CHG-gain gene analysis.

claims.claim: Among 4,769 CHG-gain genes, 4,104 have an orthologous gene encoded in the A. thaliana genome.
claims.source: Among these genes, 4,104 have an orthologous gene encoded in the A. thaliana genome, and, out of those, 1,526 were classified as gbM in the A. thaliana Col-0 accession, which is significantly more than expected by chance (p=2.83×10−222, hypergeometric test) (Supplementary file 9).
claims.evidence: This is supported by orthology analysis.

claims.claim: Out of 4,104 CHG-gain genes with A. thaliana orthologs, 1,526 were classified as gbM in the A. thaliana Col-0 accession, which is significantly more than expected by chance (p=2.83×10−222, hypergeometric test).
claims.source: Among these genes, 4,104 have an orthologous gene encoded in the A. thaliana genome, and, out of those, 1,526 were classified as gbM in the A. thaliana Col-0 accession, which is significantly more than expected by chance (p=2.83×10−222, hypergeometric test) (Supplementary file 9).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of orthology data.

claims.claim: GbM genes are generally characterized as being constitutively expressed at moderate levels.
claims.source: Relative to unmethylated genes, gbM genes are generally characterized as being constitutively expressed at moderate levels, they tend to be longer and have more exons, and have a higher frequency of CMT3-preferred CHG sites (Bewick et al., 2016; Bewick et al., 2017; Lister et al., 2008; Niederhuth et al., 2016; Takuno and Gaut, 2012; Takuno and Gaut, 2013; Takuno et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about gbM gene characteristics supported by citations.

claims.claim: GbM genes tend to be longer and have more exons.
claims.source: Relative to unmethylated genes, gbM genes are generally characterized as being constitutively expressed at moderate levels, they tend to be longer and have more exons, and have a higher frequency of CMT3-preferred CHG sites (Bewick et al., 2016; Bewick et al., 2017; Lister et al., 2008; Niederhuth et al., 2016; Takuno and Gaut, 2012; Takuno and Gaut, 2013; Takuno et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about gbM gene characteristics supported by citations.

claims.claim: GbM genes have a higher frequency of CMT3-preferred CHG sites.
claims.source: Relative to unmethylated genes, gbM genes are generally characterized as being constitutively expressed at moderate levels, they tend to be longer and have more exons, and have a higher frequency of CMT3-preferred CHG sites (Bewick et al., 2016; Bewick et al., 2017; Lister et al., 2008; Niederhuth et al., 2016; Takuno and Gaut, 2012; Takuno and Gaut, 2013; Takuno et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about gbM gene characteristics supported by citations.

claims.claim: CHG-gain genes were longer than unmethylated genes.
claims.source: On average, CHG-gain genes were longer, contained more exons, exhibited a more moderate, but on average higher, range of expression, and had a higher frequency of CHG cytosines relative to gene length compared to unmethylated genes (Figure 4B–E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: CHG-gain genes contained more exons than unmethylated genes.
claims.source: On average, CHG-gain genes were longer, contained more exons, exhibited a more moderate, but on average higher, range of expression, and had a higher frequency of CHG cytosines relative to gene length compared to unmethylated genes (Figure 4B–E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: CHG-gain genes exhibited a more moderate, but on average higher, range of expression than unmethylated genes.
claims.source: On average, CHG-gain genes were longer, contained more exons, exhibited a more moderate, but on average higher, range of expression, and had a higher frequency of CHG cytosines relative to gene length compared to unmethylated genes (Figure 4B–E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: CHG-gain genes had a higher frequency of CHG cytosines relative to gene length compared to unmethylated genes.
claims.source: On average, CHG-gain genes were longer, contained more exons, exhibited a more moderate, but on average higher, range of expression, and had a higher frequency of CHG cytosines relative to gene length compared to unmethylated genes (Figure 4B–E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: AtCMT3 in E. salsugineum methylates genes that are orthologs and/or characterized by similar properties of gbM loci in A. thaliana.
claims.source: Therefore, AtCMT3 in E. salsugineum methylates genes that are orthologs and/or characterized by similar properties of gbM loci in A. thaliana.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on orthology and gene characteristic analyses.

claims.claim: 2,094 of the 4,312 CHG DMRs overlapping CHG-gain genes had no detectable CHG methylation in wild type.
claims.source: Importantly, 2,094 of the 4,312 regions had no detectable CHG methylation in wild type and 597 of the 4,312 had no methylation in any sequence context (see also Figure 5A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by methylation analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: 597 of the 4,312 CHG DMRs overlapping CHG-gain genes had no methylation in any sequence context in wild type.
claims.source: Importantly, 2,094 of the 4,312 regions had no detectable CHG methylation in wild type and 597 of the 4,312 had no methylation in any sequence context (see also Figure 5A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by methylation analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: The CHG methylation over CHG-gain genes was highly enriched for CWG methylation, consistent with the preferred substrates of CMT3.
claims.source: Further dividing CHG methylation into CWG and CCG contexts revealed that the CHG methylation was highly enriched for CWG methylation, consistent with the preferred substrates of CMT3 (Gouil and Baulcombe, 2016; Stoddard et al., 2019) (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by trinucleotide context analysis shown in Figure 5A and cited studies.

claims.claim: The CHH methylation over CHG-gain genes was almost exclusively in the CWA context, which is indicative of CMT2 activity and not RdDM.
claims.source: Widespread, but lesser gains were also identified for CHH cytosines (Figure 5A). The CHH methylation was almost exclusively in the CWA context, which is indicative of CMT2 activity and not RdDM (Gouil and Baulcombe, 2016), suggesting that CMT3 activity likely leads to the recruitment of CMT2.
claims.evidence: This is supported by trinucleotide context analysis shown in Figure 5A and cited study.

claims.claim: CMT3 activity likely leads to the recruitment of CMT2.
claims.source: The CHH methylation was almost exclusively in the CWA context, which is indicative of CMT2 activity and not RdDM (Gouil and Baulcombe, 2016), suggesting that CMT3 activity likely leads to the recruitment of CMT2.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the CWA methylation pattern.

claims.claim: Gains in genic CG methylation occurred appreciably over most loci, including regions with no prior CG methylation.
claims.source: Gains in genic CG methylation were comparatively lower than the other sequence contexts, but did occur appreciably over most loci, including regions with no prior CG methylation (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by methylation analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: The proportional CHG methylation levels on genes mirrored AtCMT3 expression levels.
claims.source: Results showed that the proportional CHG methylation levels on genes mirrored AtCMT3 expression levels, with a slight increase in proportional methylation from 92% in AtCMT3-L2T3 to 100% (by definition) in AtCMT3-L2T4 (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Following the T4 generation, the number of CHG cytosines methylated showed a marked decrease, with only 62% of T4 levels remaining methylated in the T5 generation and 4% remaining methylated in the T6 generation.
claims.source: Following the T4 generation, and consistent with progressive silencing of the AtCMT3 transgene, the number of CHG cytosines methylated showed a marked decrease, with only 62% of T4 levels remaining methylated in the T5 generation and 4% remaining methylated in the T6 generation where AtCMT3 expression was greatly reduced (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: CHH context cytosines showed a similar trend to CHG with 97% cytosines methylated in the T3 relative to the T4 generation, followed by a steep decline, with only 24% and 5% methylated remaining in the T5 and T6 generations, respectively.
claims.source: CHH context cytosines showed a similar trend with 97% cytosines methylated in the T3 relative to the T4 generation, followed by a steep decline, with only 24% and 5% methylated remaining in the T5 and T6 generations, respectively, relative to the T4 (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: CG context cytosines showed a more substantial increase from the T3 to T4 generation, with CG cytosines in the T3 generation at 54% of the levels measured in T4.
claims.source: CG context cytosines showed a more substantial increase from the T3 to T4 generation, with CG cytosines in the T3 generation at 54% of the levels measured in T4 (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Following the T4 generation, the proportion of methylated CG sites remaining following the progressive AtCMT3 silencing was relatively high and much more stable, with 68% in T5% and 51% in T6 of the CG cytosines remaining methylated, relative to T4.
claims.source: Also contrasting with CHG and CHH methylation, following the T4 generation, the proportion of methylated CG sites remaining following the progressive AtCMT3 silencing was relatively high and much more stable, with 68% in T5% and 51% in T6 of the CG cytosines remaining methylated, relative to T4 (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: In AtCMT3-L1, the relative methylation levels were maintained in all sequence contexts across generations.
claims.source: The results of the analysis of genic methylation for AtCMT3-L2 contrast with the identical analysis conducted on AtCMT3-L1, which did not show evidence of silencing of the AtCMT3 transgene. In this case, the relative methylation levels were maintained in all sequence contexts across generations (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: In the F2 progeny that did not encode the transgene, the ectopic genic CHG and CHH methylation that was present in the transgenic parent was lost but the genic CG methylation was maintained.
claims.source: In the F2 progeny that did not encode the transgene, the ectopic genic CHG and CHH methylation that was present in the in the transgenic parent was lost but the genic CG methylation was maintained, similar to the result from AtCMT3-L2 when the transgene was silenced (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: The F2 progeny that still encoded the transgene maintained similar levels of genic methylation in all contexts as the transgenic parent.
claims.source: In contrast, the F2 progeny that still encoded the transgene maintained similar levels of genic methylation in all contexts as the transgenic parent (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: The levels of newly methylated CG cytosines on CHG-gain genes in lines that lost AtCMT3 were higher than background due to bisulfite non-conversion.
claims.source: Importantly, the levels of newly methylated CG cytosines on CHG-gain genes in both the lines that lost AtCMT3 through silencing or crossing out were higher than background due to bisulfite non-conversion, estimated by comparing them to randomly sampled, un-methylated genes that did not gain CHG methylation (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-B.

claims.claim: The genic CG methylation is unlikely to have occurred independently of AtCMT3.
claims.source: The genic CG methylation is also unlikely to have occurred independently of AtCMT3, as the gains in genic CG methylation at these loci are also higher that those found by comparing an additional, non-transgenic E. salsugineum accession (Yukon) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison to a non-transgenic accession shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-B.

claims.claim: Genic CG methylation showed a lesser dependency on AtCMT3 expression and was preferentially maintained following loss of transgene expression.
claims.source: Thus, genic CG methylation showed a lesser dependency on AtCMT3 expression and was preferentially maintained following loss of transgene expression, either through natural silencing or crossing out the transgene, consistent with maintenance of CG methylation by other methyltransferases recruited by initial AtCMT3 activity.

results.result: Expression of AtCMT3 in E. salsugineum reconstitutes gene body methylation through a progression from de novo CHG methylation to stable CG methylation. AtCMT3 expression resulted in CHG methylation over genes with no prior methylation (C40, C42, C52, C63, C64), particularly at CWG sites (C104), followed by accumulation of CG methylation (C5, C48, C107, C111) and CHH methylation in CWA context (C105). The number of CHG-gain genes correlated with AtCMT3 expression levels (C58, C71). Following transgene silencing or crossing out, CG methylation was preferentially maintained (51-68% retention) while CHG and CHH methylation were largely lost (4-5% retention) (C49, C109, C112, C114), demonstrating that CMT3 initiates heritable CG epimutations (C6, C50, C129).
results.evaluation: The claims are strongly supported by comprehensive whole-genome bisulfite sequencing data across multiple generations (C51-C73), showing temporal progression of methylation patterns. The correlation between AtCMT3 expression and methylation levels is statistically significant (R²=0.88, p=1.67×10⁻⁴) (C58). The preferential maintenance of CG methylation after transgene loss is demonstrated through both natural silencing and genetic crosses (C114-C115), with appropriate controls comparing to unmethylated genes and non-transgenic accessions (C116-C117). The trinucleotide context analysis confirms CMT3 substrate specificity (C104-C105).

results.result: CHG methylation at gene bodies occurs independently of stable H3K9me2 and does not cause transcriptional silencing. Regions enriched for H3K9me2 in wild type showed increased CHG methylation in AtCMT3 lines (C74), but genes gaining CHG methylation had no pre-existing H3K9me2 (C76) and did not accumulate stable H3K9me2 or H3K9me1 after CHG methylation (C77, C79, C80). CHG-gain genes showed no significant expression changes (C45, C82-C85), and genic CHG methylation was uncoupled from transcriptional silencing (C90), likely due to IBM1 demethylase activity (C47, C139, C140).
results.evaluation: The claims are well-supported by ChIP-seq data for both H3K9me2 and H3K9me1 across multiple generations (C74-C81), combined with RNA-seq data showing minimal expression changes in CHG-gain genes (C82-C85). The lack of H3K9me enrichment over CHG-gain genes is clearly demonstrated in metaplots (Figure 3C-F), and the presence of IBM1 orthologs in E. salsugineum provides a mechanistic explanation (C139). However, the claim that IBM1 is the cause (C47, C140) remains speculative as no direct functional evidence is provided.

results.result: CHG-gain genes in E. salsugineum are orthologs of A. thaliana gbM genes and share similar characteristics. Among 4,769 CHG-gain genes, 4,104 have A. thaliana orthologs, with 1,526 (37%) classified as gbM genes—significantly more than expected by chance (p=2.83×10⁻²²²) (C93). CHG-gain genes are longer (C97), have more exons (C98), show moderate but higher expression levels (C99), and have higher CHG site frequency (C100) compared to unmethylated genes, matching known characteristics of gbM genes (C94-C96).
results.evaluation: The orthology analysis is well-supported with appropriate statistical testing (hypergeometric test, p=2.83×10⁻²²²) (C93). The gene characteristic comparisons use appropriate non-parametric tests (Wilcoxon rank-sum) and show statistically significant differences (p-values provided in Figure 4B-E) (C97-C100). The comparison to established gbM characteristics is supported by multiple citations (C94-C96). The convergence of orthology and functional characteristics provides strong evidence for the conclusion (C101).

results.result: AtCMT3 preferentially targets heterochromatin over genes, with differential methylation maintenance after transgene loss. In heterochromatin (repeats/intergenic regions), 55-57% of CHG/CHH methylation and 66% of CG methylation remained in T6 despite low AtCMT3 expression (C121, C123), compared to only 4-5% CHG/CHH and 51% CG retention in genes (C122). The majority of CHG DMRs (78%) overlapped repetitive elements or intergenic regions (C61), which showed 15% to 30-70% CHG methylation increases (C62). This differential maintenance suggests AtCMT3 preferentially targets heterochromatin and requires high expression levels to methylate genes (C128).
results.evaluation: The claims are supported by systematic comparison of methylation maintenance between genic and heterochromatic regions across generations (Figure 5B-C) (C120-C123). The differential retention is quantitatively documented with appropriate controls. The crossing experiments provide additional support (C124-C125). However, the interpretation that residual AtCMT3 preferentially targets heterochromatin (C127) versus alternative explanations (e.g., differential maintenance by other pathways) (C126) requires more direct evidence. The conclusion about expression level requirements (C128) is reasonable but somewhat inferential.

results.result: The authors propose a mechanistic model where gbM originates from simultaneous targeting by euchromatin and heterochromatin pathways, priming genes for stable CG epimutations. The model posits that rare incorporation of H3K9me1-marked nucleosomes into transcribed genes (C135, C136) allows CMT3 binding and de novo CHG methylation (C141), which transiently stabilizes H3K9me2 and recruits additional methyltransferases like CMT2 (C143). IBM1 removes H3K9me2 (C144), disrupting non-CG methylation maintenance, but CG methylation persists via MET1 (C145). This makes gbM a passive byproduct of heterochromatin machinery spillage into genic space (C146, C150).
results.evaluation: This is a proposed mechanistic model that integrates the experimental findings with prior knowledge, but many components remain speculative (C135, C136, C141-C145). While the model is consistent with the data showing: (1) de novo CHG methylation at genes, (2) lack of stable H3K9me2, (3) recruitment of CMT2 (CWA methylation), and (4) preferential CG maintenance, several key steps lack direct experimental validation in this study. The role of H3K9me1 (C136), the transient stabilization of H3K9me2 (C141), and the specific mechanism of CMT2 recruitment (C143) are inferred rather than demonstrated. The model requires additional functional experiments to test specific predictions.

results.result: Background on gene body methylation and CMT3. GbM is characterized by CG-context methylation on expressed genes in many plant species (C1, C11), maintained by MET1 (C29), but species lacking gbM also lack CMT3 (C2, C32), leading to the hypothesis that CMT3 is required for gbM establishment (C33). E. salsugineum, which diverged from A. thaliana ~47 million years ago (C38), has lost both CMT3 and gbM (C37), making it suitable for testing CMT3's role in gbM establishment.
results.evaluation: These are well-established background claims supported by extensive citations (C1, C2, C11-C13, C28-C29, C32-C33, C37-C38). The phylogenetic relationship and loss of CMT3/gbM in E. salsugineum are documented in cited comparative genomic studies. The hypothesis that CMT3 is required for gbM establishment (C33) is appropriately presented as a hypothesis to be tested, not as established fact. The choice of E. salsugineum as an experimental system is well-justified.

results.result: Background on plant DNA methylation pathways. The RdDM pathway uses DRM2 for de novo methylation in all contexts (C14-C15), MET1 maintains CG methylation at hemi-methylated sites (C16-C17), CMT3 maintains CHG methylation with preference for CWG sites (C18-C19), and CMT2 targets CHH methylation with CWA enrichment (C20-C21). CMT2 and CMT3 participate in a feedback loop with H3K9me2 (C23-C25), resulting in co-dependent losses in mutants (C26-C27).
results.evaluation: These are well-established facts about plant DNA methylation pathways, each supported by appropriate citations to primary literature (C14-C27). The mechanistic details about substrate preferences (C19, C21), feedback loops (C23-C25), and mutant phenotypes (C26-C27) are documented in the cited studies. This background information is accurate and provides necessary context for interpreting the experimental results.

results.result: Examples of epimutations with phenotypic consequences. Differential methylation causes peloric mutants in toadflax (bilateral to radial flower symmetry) (C9) and affects fruit ripening at the colorless non-ripening locus in tomato (C10).
results.evaluation: These are well-documented examples from the literature, supported by appropriate citations (Cubas et al., 1999; Manning et al., 2006). These examples provide motivation for studying epimutation mechanisms but are not part of the current study's results.

results.result: CHG-gain genes show minimal expression changes unrelated to AtCMT3. Only ≤10% of CHG-gain genes showed >2 log2 fold expression changes, with similar numbers up- and down-regulated (C82-C83). There was no correlation between CHG methylation levels and expression changes (C84), and CHG-gain genes were not enriched in differentially expressed genes (p>0.05) (C85). GO enrichment analysis showed stress response terms but no consistent patterns across lineages (C86-C87), suggesting AtCMT3 expression was not the cause of expression changes (C88).
results.evaluation: The RNA-seq analysis is comprehensive with appropriate statistical testing (Fisher's exact test, p>0.05) (C85) and multiple lines analyzed (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1). The lack of correlation between methylation and expression is clearly shown (C84). The GO enrichment analysis appropriately notes the lack of consistency across lineages (C87), supporting the conclusion that expression changes are not directly caused by AtCMT3 (C88). However, the 2 log2 fold change threshold is somewhat arbitrary, and more subtle expression effects cannot be ruled out.
